Oct 20 : It was a difficult, almost incomprehensible, feat. A band of seafarers from Easter Island in the South Pacific set off in double-hulled sailing canoes on a voyage across Earth's largest ocean that ended more than 4,400 miles (7,100 km) away in Hawaii, the only Polynesian island in the Northern Hemisphere. But this oceanic odyssey centuries ago was no myth. New genetic research has determined that Native Hawaiians are genetically most closely related to the people of Easter Island, also called Rapa Nui. "Using whole genomes, our algorithms can find DNA sequences matching perfectly between individuals on different islands, the legacy of common ancestors. From these data we can create family trees of the islands," said Stanford University computational geneticist Alexander Ioannidis, co-senior author of the study published in the journal Science.  The findings point to a founding population of people from Easter Island arriving in Hawaii as the first humans to settle the lush volcanic island chain.

The data indicated that the people who settled Easter Island arrived there in the 1200s after journeying from Mangareva island in French Polynesia, more than 1,500 miles (2,400 km) away, and that a subset of them subsequently set off for Hawaii. That voyage likely occurred in the same century, Ioannidis said. "We examined shared segments of DNA, genetic variation and thousands of reconstructed family trees. In 61 per cent of those trees, Hawaii and Rapa Nui were paired together. We checked it four different ways because, frankly, we were dumbfounded and couldn't believe it ourselves at first," said genome scientist and study co-senior author Keolu Fox of the University of California, San Diego. It would have been an incredible journey, Ioannidis said. "In their canoes, they brought with them plants that they would need on the newly settled island, and they included bananas, taro and sweet potato, as well as animals like the chicken. It is believed that the Polynesians would embark on these voyages across thousands of miles of ocean in order to discover new islands rich in resources and land to settle," Ioannidis said. The researchers pieced together these long-ago journeys based on genetic data revealing the relatedness of present-day people from various Polynesian islands, analyzing DNA from more than 1,000 Polynesian people. These included 317 Native Hawaiians, 12 Rapa Nui and 8 Mangarevans, as well as others from the Society, Tuamotu, Marquesas, Austral, Samoan and Tongan islands. The genetic data showed Mangarevan ancestry was second only to Easter Island ancestry for Native Hawaiians. MONUMENTAL SEA CROSSINGS The researchers attribute these monumental sea crossings to an ultravoyaging population they call Holomoana Nui, the Hawaiian phrase for "great ocean voyaging," with Hawaii as the last destination reached. They were the greatest voyaging community in human history, according to Fox, who is a Native Hawaiian. "Polynesians were exploring and settling the Pacific centuries before Europeans began their celebrated voyages of discovery," Fox said. "Perhaps it's time to rethink who we call explorers." Using genetic data, the researchers previously tracked how Polynesian voyagers reached a succession of islands over a period of centuries in one of the most impressive settlement feats in human history, but that study traced them only as far as Easter Island. THE FOUNDING OF TAHITI The new study included a detailed genomic analysis of people from Tahiti, one of the Society Islands and the locale for which the researchers had the most genomes. They were able to estimate the size and date of the founding generation — roughly 800 people reaching Tahiti around the year 1070. "Since the voyage to Hawaii was much longer, we would expect its founding population size to have been no larger and likely smaller," Ioannidis said. Native Hawaiians and Easter Islanders share many cultural traits found among eastern Polynesians, including a similar Austronesian language and similar foods, Ioannidis said. The study has implications for disease risk among Native Hawaiians and other Polynesians due to genetic bottlenecks called "founder effects." These arise when a small portion of a population separates and founds a new population, as the Polynesians did each time they ventured to and settled on a new island. This narrowing of the gene pool can amplify the frequency of some rare genetic variants sometimes related to diseases, while others vanish entirely, Ioannidis said. The Polynesians repeated the pattern of settling on new lands, intensifying the effect. "Repeated founder effects concentrated rare disease-associated variants in Polynesian populations. We identified variants linked to kidney disease and blindness that occur at surprisingly high frequencies in French Polynesia," Fox said. Founder effects have been extensively studied in certain populations including the Amish, Ashkenazi Jews and Finns, leading to standard screenings for certain genetic conditions for them. "Why not Hawaiians?" Fox asked.

Oct 20 : Salesforce said on Tuesday it would acquire Braze in a deal valued at about $5.66 billion, eyeing the New York-based company's AI-driven personalization tools to strengthen its business software offerings. The deal is the latest bet by Salesforce to accelerate its AI transition as investors worry that the rapid adoption of the technology could erode demand for traditional software. Braze Class A shareholders will receive $47.50 in cash per share held, representing a premium of about 58.1 per cent to the stock's last close. Shares of Braze jumped more than 50 per cent in early trading while Salesforce's stock dipped.

NEW YORK, Oct 20 : The US dollar slipped on Tuesday as doubts over the AI trade resurfaced, while the euro edged up despite traders' lingering worries about unrest in France. Shares in South Korean AI services firm Elice Group plunged 32 per cent in their Seoul market debut, a sign that negative sentiment toward the AI sector in global markets is not easing. Strong capital inflows into US stocks have supported the dollar. Higher interest rates, driven partly by growth and inflation expectations tied to the sector, have also helped. "The dollar has been supported by big inflows into the equity market," said Dominic Bunning, head of G10 FX strategy at Nomura.

The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, fell 0.27 per cent to 101.69, with the euro up 0.2 per cent at $1.1232. Traders remained wary of the euro despite Tuesday's modest gains as France faces widespread protests and a worsening fiscal picture. The government said overnight curfews in violence-hit areas of France's biggest cities had brought some respite from the country's worst unrest in years. More protests are planned for the weekend. "The worries in France are not going away anytime soon," said Tommy von Brömsen, FX strategist at Handelsbanken. "The bearish view on France will stay for a while longer, and there's much more euro weakness to be priced in." Britain's pound strengthened 0.66 per cent to $1.339 after labour market data showed a resilient jobs market, the latest batch of data from the UK that surprised to the upside. "The risk is that a resilient labour market gives the Bank of England both the room and the reason to raise interest rates again," said Lale Akoner, global market strategist at eToro. "Sterling could benefit from rising rate expectations." Markets are almost fully pricing in a 25-basis-point rate hike by the Bank of England at its next meeting on November 5, according to LSEG data. STRONG JAPANESE BOND AUCTION The yen jumped after an auction of longer-dated Japanese government bonds (JGBs) drew record demand.  "The record 20-year auction is a strong signal that sidelined cash is finally coming back," said Masahiko Loo, senior fixed-income strategist at State Street Investment Management in Tokyo. "JGBs are also starting to look like a relative haven from Europe's political and fiscal volatility, particularly around France.” The Japanese yen gained 0.29 per cent against the greenback to 158.04 per dollar.  Elsewhere, the Canadian dollar rose 0.42 per cent to 1.405 per US dollar, its strongest level in almost a month, after Alberta residents voted by a large majority to remain part of Canada in the province's first-ever referendum on separation.

Oct 20 : Qualcomm will cut jobs globally in a "performance-focused reduction" following its annual employee reviews, CEO Cristiano Amon told staff in a memo on Monday reviewed by Reuters, with notifications set to begin in November. The cuts are part of an effort to build "a stronger performance culture" and address situations where the company "has consistently fallen short of expectations," Amon said. The memo did not say how many jobs would be affected, and Reuters could not immediately determine the scale of the cuts. Qualcomm did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It had about 52,000 employees globally as of September last year, most of them full-time. Its financial year typically ends in late September.

One of the world's biggest smartphone chipmakers, Qualcomm has been hit this year by a slump in consumer electronics sales as soaring memory prices weigh on demand in key markets. Its shares have risen just 1.5 per cent in 2026, compared with gains of more than 12 per cent for the benchmark S&P 500 and nearly 60 per cent for the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index. Qualcomm shares were up more than 1 per cent after trading down about 0.5 per cent earlier on Tuesday. In its latest earnings report in late July, Qualcomm forecast quarterly profit below estimates and said revenue from Apple products would decline faster than expected, while signaling that growth in data-center and other non-handset businesses would more than offset the lost revenue by fiscal 2027. The company expects the majority of its chip sales to come from businesses other than smartphones in fiscal 2027 as it expands into the fast-growing AI data-center market. Amon said in the memo business priorities, organizational needs, skills and expertise would be considered in making the cuts. "As we have expanded the business, so have the competencies and skills we require," he wrote. "We must have the right people in the right roles so they can perform at their best and the company can continue to succeed."

Oct 20 : Toymaker Hasbro raised full-year forecast for both overall revenue and its digital gaming business on Tuesday, as its flagship trading card game, "Magic: The Gathering", powers demand ahead of the crucial holiday season. The Play-Doh maker has posted seven straight quarters of gains in digital gaming, which also includes Monopoly Go!, while stronger sales of collectibles linked to Marvel, K-Pop Demon Hunters and Transformers boosted demand for traditional toys. Its shares were up 5 per cent. The Wizards of the Coast and Digital Gaming segment, the company's second-largest revenue generator, grew 31 per cent during the third quarter. Revenue from the consumer products segment rose 4 per cent. Quarterly revenue from "Magic: The Gathering" gaming franchise topped $600 million for the first time, up 34 per cent from a year earlier, fueled by premiere sets — The Hobbit and Reality Fracture.

LONDON, Oct 20 : Britain's competition regulator said on Tuesday it was seeking to loosen Apple's grip on contactless payments by proposing that the company lower fees and remove technical barriers, helping rival services compete with Apple Pay. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said its proposals would result in "substantially lower access fees" and easier access to Apple's contactless technology. The measures are less onerous than those imposed by the European Union in 2024, which included free access for third-party developers. Companies including PayPal, Klarna, Curve and BBVA have since launched alternative payment apps, the CMA said. 'HIGH FEES, STRICT TERMS'

The EU commitments require Apple to give wallet developers access to the iPhone's NFC chip using host card emulation (HCE), allowing third-party apps to process contactless payments without going through Apple Pay or Apple Wallet. The CMA's proposals would give developers access to HCE in addition to Apple's existing secure element (SE) technology. The regulator can impose requirements on Apple after designating it and Google as having strategic market status in smartphones last year. Contactless payments account for 39 per cent of all payments, compared with 3 per cent a decade ago, the CMA said. More than 60 per cent of adults use a digital wallet, with Apple Wallet the most popular in Britain. CMA Chief Executive Sarah Cardell said the proposals would boost innovation, consumer choice and Britain's fintech sector. "We have heard that high fees, strict terms, and technical restrictions relating to Apple's contactless technology make it too difficult for challengers to innovate and compete," she said. The CMA is consulting on the proposals until November 17, before making a final decision. Digital bank Revolut welcomed the proposals, saying access to NFC technology through HCE was critical. "The CMA's direction creates a real opportunity for UK fintechs to compete on an equal footing with Big Tech," said Revolut's chief commercial officer, David Tirado. Apple said developers could already offer contactless payments through its NFC technology and secure element, which stores sensitive information such as card credentials and cryptographic keys. It said this enabled services including in-store payments, transit passes and event tickets while protecting users' data. "We do not believe the CMA should require Apple to adopt an approach with lower privacy and security protections," an Apple spokesperson said. "We will continue to engage constructively to reach an outcome that is in the best interest of our users."

Services for the digital bank Revolut, including withdrawals from ATMs, bank transfers and bank card top-ups, were disrupted, which a source close to the matter attributed to the Google Cloud failures. UK lenders Lloyds and HSBC confirmed that customers faced issues with their banking services.  "We understand the root issues have been resolved, so we expect all our services to be back to normal soon," Lloyds said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. Internet service tracker Downdetector indicated that hundreds of reports had been made of problems affecting business in the UK, including the property website Rightmove, delivery service DPD and the Royal Mail postal service. Commentary: An Amazon outage has rattled the internet – why the ‘cloud’ needs to change

RELIANCE ON HYPERSCALERS Google said it would publish a full incident report in the coming days.  The outage has renewed concerns over the global reliance on cloud providers, which offer businesses on-demand IT resources without heavy investment in expensive server farms. Local providers have seen their share of the market shrink in recent years and been captured by foreign giants known as 'hyperscalers'. A global outage at Amazon's cloud services last year disrupted many online services for video games, business and transport firms and made part of the internet inaccessible for several hours. Only three major hyperscalers -- Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services -- have the infrastructure to handle vast amounts of data needed by businesses at scale in the UK, said University of Surrey cybersecurity professor Alan Woodward. These centres remain "susceptible to localised infrastructure failures", which can have significant knock-on effects when so many businesses depend on just a handful of providers, he added. He said the problem is "intensifying with the AI boom" as demand for hyperscalers rises, meaning "we are becoming more reliant on these few massive entities".

MILAN, Oct 20 : Smart glasses that resemble ordinary eyewear are under increased scrutiny from European regulators and advocacy groups, leaving investors questioning whether sales can keep booming as Ray-Ban maker EssilorLuxottica reports third-quarter results. EssilorLuxottica launched its Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses, capable of filming and recording, in 2023 and the market has grown rapidly. Global shipments of AI-enabled glasses jumped to 8.4 million units in 2025 from around 2.1 million in 2024, according to research group Omdia. EssilorLuxottica's Meta eyewear accounted for 81.3 per cent of global shipments in the first half of this year. When it releases its third-quarter results on Tuesday, EssilorLuxottica is not expected to give precise data on the value of smart glasses sales, but may provide an indication. In its second-quarter trading update, it said smart glasses sales nearly doubled compared to the same period a year earlier.

SOME GOVERNMENTS CONSIDER BANS The resemblance to ordinary eyewear has been a factor in the success of EssilorLuxottica's Meta smart glasses, and is in contrast to Google Glass more than a decade ago, whose bulky, futuristic design limited mainstream consumer appeal. But the design's discretion is troubling to regulators. Last week, the European Data Protection Board, or EDPB, which brings together national privacy regulators, said the devices facilitated covert recording, including of bystanders' conversations. Louis Larere, portfolio manager at French asset manager BDL, echoed that concern. "The fact that smart glasses include a camera, allow users to livestream and instantly share content on social media could become a problem," he said. So far Norway has taken the toughest stance among governments, saying earlier this month it planned a temporary ban on the use of AI glasses in selected locations. Australia said in September it was considering barring the use of camera-equipped smart glasses in government workplaces. In a preliminary, non-binding statement, the EDPB urged manufacturers to combine measures such as visible recording lights, sound alerts and notifications to nearby devices while recording. The authority also suggested limiting live streaming, automatically blurring bystanders' faces and using location-based technical restrictions in sensitive settings like hospitals or schools. PRIVACY CONCERNS MAY LIMIT ADOPTION Ross Gerber, CEO of California-based wealth management firm Gerber Kawasaki, which holds Meta shares, said privacy concerns and social stigma could limit wider adoption even though smart glasses still hold long-term potential. "People will make you feel uncomfortable if you wear them, and people feel uncomfortable wearing them because of this," he said, adding that his pair of Meta glasses was sitting unused in his garage. A Meta spokesperson said the glasses remain popular for music, calls and live translations. "They were built to be noticed which is why every pair with a camera has a bright light on the front that flashes when you take a photo or video you can share with others," they added. "It's important that rules protect people's rights while supporting innovation and consistency across technologies," an EssilorLuxottica spokesperson told Reuters, adding that the company is working to help consumers understand how to use the glasses responsibly and respectfully. Data regulators in Italy and Austria both told Reuters that they were investigating incidents involving smart glasses being used by pupils in schools, and France's data watchdog previously said it had received a small number of complaints. "Authorities should think about banning these devices in public spaces in a more coordinated manner," Kleanthi Sardeli, a lawyer at European digital rights advocacy group NOYB, told Reuters. Growing privacy concerns could pose a challenge for EssilorLuxottica and Meta as they seek to position AI glasses, which can be used for making calls and listening to music, as a potential future alternative to smartphones. "(Privacy concerns) are a risk to this category. We already saw something similar more than a decade ago with Google Glasses," Cedric Rossi, luxury and consumer goods equity research analyst at Stifel, said. Rossi said Meta's unveiling in September of camera-free audio glasses was a first step toward addressing regulatory and privacy concerns. However, he added that, without a camera, users cannot fully benefit from the AI capabilities the devices are designed to offer. Other companies, meanwhile, are still drawn to the category and Google, in partnership with Samsung, plans to release its Gemini AI glasses before the end of this year. Apple is also expected to release its own smart glasses. BofA analysts in a report this month assessed the regulatory risk as limited and that an outright ban was unlikely even if additional restrictions emerge, particularly in Europe.

TOKYO, Oct 20 : The Bank of Japan may raise its inflation outlook for the next fiscal year in forecasts due this month, as rising oil prices exert longer-than-expected price pressures on the economy, four sources familiar with the central bank's thinking said. Having just raised interest rates last month, the BOJ is expected to keep rates steady at the two-day policy meeting ending on October 30, unless the yen renews its slide that lifts import costs and broader inflation, the sources said. But the central bank will likely maintain its focus on mounting inflationary risks in a quarterly report due after the meeting, the sources said, leaving scope for another rate hike as soon as December. "Consumer price growth may stay elevated for longer than expected, though there's no big change in underlying inflation," said one of the sources, a view echoed by two other sources.

"Inflation pressures exist but haven't jumped, so there's little reason to rush," another source said on the timing of the next rate hike. The sources spoke on condition of anonymity as they were not authorised to speak publicly. The BOJ was not immediately available for comment. In forecasts made in July, the BOJ projected core consumer inflation hitting 2.5 per cent in the current fiscal year ending in March 2027, before slowing to 2.4 per cent the following year. The projections assumed that the pass-through of the initial spike in fuel costs would moderate from the latter half of next year. In new forecasts due this month, the board may slightly revise up its core inflation forecast for fiscal 2027 to reflect the pass-through from the recent, renewed spike in crude oil prices, the sources said. Any revisions will be minor with little sign that dangerous second-round effects, in which the energy shock triggers a spiral of sharp wage and price rises, are becoming embedded in the economy, they said. The board is likely to roughly maintain its economic forecasts projecting growth of 0.6 per cent in fiscal 2026 and 0.8 per cent in 2027, with robust exports of AI-related goods offsetting soft consumption, the sources said. The BOJ is unlikely to incorporate the expected impact of a two-year cut to a consumption tax on food items scheduled from April next year, as a bill to put the move into effect has yet to pass parliament, they said. FINANCIAL CONDITIONS KEY The BOJ raised its key rate to a 31-year high of 1.25 per cent last month, signalling its entry into a phase focused on preventing underlying inflation from overshooting its target and raising the prospect of tighter policy. BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda has warned that underlying inflation, or the broad price trend stripping away temporary, one-off factors, may overshoot its 2 per cent target on price pressures from the Middle East conflict, a weak yen and brisk AI demand. With underlying inflation having roughly hit 2 per cent, the BOJ will likely emphasise in the upcoming report its focus on anchoring inflation around its target, the sources said, a sign of its readiness to keep raising rates steadily. The central bank is also expected to maintain its view that financial conditions remain accommodative, suggesting further scope for rate hikes, the sourcdes said. Still, recent data suggests inflation risks are not heightening in a way that warrants a back-to-back rate hike. While wages will keep rising next year, a big jump is unlikely as government fuel subsidies moderate the pace of increase in this year's consumer inflation - the base for which unions negotiate pay with companies next year, analysts say. Corporate inflation expectations remained elevated but did not accelerate from three months earlier, the BOJ's "tankan" survey showed on October 1, taking some pressure off the central bank to follow a hike in September with another in October. Many analysts polled by Reuters expect the BOJ to raise its policy rate twice to 1.75 per cent by June next year, with respondents' bets on the terminal rate centering around 1.75 per cent to 2 per cent.

ZURICH, Oct 20 : ABB dropped nearly 6 per cent on Tuesday as market nervousness about the sustainability of investments in artificial intelligence weighed on the Swiss engineering company, which is a major supplier to data centres. Record new orders and an increase in its full-year sales guidance failed to appease institutional buy-side investors who were looking for more, analysts said, as AI-linked stocks fell more broadly. On South Korea's stock market, which has become one of the clearest measures of AI sentiment, traders sold heavily on Tuesday as concern mounted over rising costs. While European semiconductor stocks also fell, ABB shares fell more than peers. The stock, which reached its highest level to date of 89.14 Swiss francs ($108.13) in June, dropped to 70.72 Swiss francs on the Swiss exchange after the results.

Investors question whether these companies get the revenues they need in the future to survive,” he said. Orders surged 40 per cent to $12 billion in the three months ended September 30, with data centres the biggest driver. The company raised its full-year sales outlook and also announced a pending $495 million investment in a joint venture with Mitsubishi Electric. "We see a continued acceleration in the market when we're looking at the demand for the build-out of data centres," Wierod told reporters.
